Impact-Driven Vision: We focus on picking a challenge where we can build a realistic, functional prototype or data visualizer—not just a theoretical idea.

Collaborative & Agile Culture: We respect everyone's time, communicate clearly, and foster an environment where every team member's voice is heard.

Goal-Oriented: We are here to learn, push our boundaries, and aim for top submission standards in the competition!
summary: Earth Trend Detective is a web dashboard that separates real environmental trends from noise in NASA Earth data. It combines a 3D globe with a switchable heatmap, 22 cities and 25 years of NASA POWER data. It compares monthly or yearly cycle amplitude of temperature, aerosols (AOD) and NO2, screens variable pairs for correlation, and produces a one-page brief where every number carries a trust grade. This addresses the challenge “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!”: visualize how Earth science variables change over time and determine what, where and how much is changing, and whether it is significant. NASA POWER provides the daily record, NASA GIBS the satellite layers behind the heatmap, and NASA FIRMS active-fire context. Signals are de-seasonalised, tested with Mann-Kendall and Sen’s slope, and corrected for multiple testing, so a short spike stays “suggestive” until it survives. In our data, none of 32 variable-pair tests passes the correlation screen, and the tool says so. This matters because a hot week or a smoky month is easily mistaken for climate change. By showing which changes are real and how strong the evidence is, the tool helps the public use open NASA data responsibly.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Earth Trend Detective lets users pick a variable, see how it changes over time, and learn what is changing, where, by how much and whether the change is statistically significant. A 3D globe shows a heatmap for the chosen variable, with notable cities ranked beside it. For each city, a Python backend de-seasonalises the series, tests the trend with Mann-Kendall and Sen’s slope, and corrects for multiple testing with Benjamini-Hochberg control. Users can compare monthly or yearly cycle amplitude of temperature, aerosols (AOD) and NO2. They can also generate a one-page brief where each number carries a trust grade from five checks.

What benefits does it have?
It turns raw Earth data into plain-language verdicts. Users see the strength of the evidence, not just a chart, and can tell a real trend from a short spike. The interface works in English and Vietnamese.

What is the intended impact?
We want students, journalists and the public to read environmental data critically. A hot week should not be reported as climate change unless the evidence supports it, and the tool should say clearly when it does not.

What tools and technologies did we use?

  • Backend: Python with FastAPI.
  • Frontend: vanilla JavaScript, Leaflet, Plotly and a custom canvas 3D globe.
  • NASA data: NASA POWER for daily weather, NASA GIBS for satellite imagery layers, and NASA FIRMS for active fires.
  • Quality: automated tests, plus a preprocessing step that checks correlations.
  • Hardware: no special hardware.

How is it creative?
We framed the analysis as detective work: every signal is a suspect and must pass tests before we call it a trend. A satellite-textured globe with a toggleable heatmap makes the data explorable. We also report negative results openly. In our data, none of 32 variable-pair tests passes the correlation screen, and the tool says so.

What factors did we consider?

  • Seasonality, which can hide or fake a real change.
  • Testing many cities and indicators at once, which inflates false positives.
  • Autocorrelation in monthly series, which we handle with an effective sample size.
  • Weak evidence, which we label as weak rather than hiding it.
  • Reliability, with cached data and an offline mock mode.
  • Accessibility for non-experts, through plain-language text and two languages.
